blocks.title: Thinking Like an Attacker
blocks.subtitle: How authorised security testing finds weaknesses before criminals do

blocks.text:
Hacking, in its original sense, means understanding a system well enough to make it do something its designers did not intend. Ethical hackers apply that skill with permission, to find weaknesses so that they can be fixed.

The techniques resemble a criminal's. What differs is authorisation, scope and what happens to the findings. Testing a system without its owner's written permission is illegal in most countries.

blocks.heading: A structured engagement
blocks.text: A penetration test is a planned exercise, not a free-for-all. The owner and the tester agree in writing what may be tested, when and how. The tester then gathers information, looks for weaknesses, demonstrates their impact in a controlled way and reports each finding with evidence and a recommended fix.

steps.text: **Authorise and scope.** A signed agreement defines the targets, methods, timing and contacts. Nothing outside it is touched.
**Understand the target.** The tester maps what is exposed: systems, services, applications and the people who use them.
**Find and confirm.** Possible weaknesses are identified and carefully confirmed, avoiding damage or disruption.
**Report and fix.** Findings are ranked by risk, explained clearly and retested after the owner has fixed them.

blocks.heading: The same few mistakes
blocks.text: Most successful attacks use well-known weaknesses: software that was never updated, passwords that are weak or reused, input that an application trusts without checking, services exposed by mistake and people persuaded to give access away. Defenders who patch promptly, enforce multi-factor authentication and validate input remove most of an attacker's options.

items.title: Vulnerability
items.text: A weakness in design, code or configuration that could be misused.

items.title: Exploit
items.text: A technique that takes advantage of a specific vulnerability.

items.title: Social engineering
items.text: Manipulating people, rather than machines, into granting access.

items.title: Patch
items.text: An update that corrects a vulnerability. Applying patches quickly is the single most effective defence.

items.title: Red team and blue team
items.text: Attack simulators and defenders, exercising against each other to improve.

items.title: Responsible disclosure
items.text: Reporting a flaw privately to the owner and allowing time to fix it before publication.

blocks.text: The difference between an attacker and a security tester is one document: written permission.

blocks.heading: Ethics and law
blocks.text: Skills that protect can also harm. Ethical practice means working only with authorisation, staying inside the agreed scope, protecting any data encountered, and reporting honestly. Many organisations run bug-bounty or disclosure programmes that welcome reports from independent researchers. Learn in legal practice environments built for training, never on systems you do not own.

items.title: Enterprise testing
items.text: Regular assessment of networks and applications.

items.title: Secure development
items.text: Finding flaws before software is released.

items.title: Critical infrastructure
items.text: Testing the systems that run power, water and transport.

blocks.question: What must exist before any penetration test begins?
options: Written authorisation and an agreed scope
blocks.explanation: Without the owner's permission, testing is unauthorised access, whatever the intent.

blocks.question: Which defence removes the largest number of known attack routes?
blocks.explanation: Most attacks use vulnerabilities for which a patch already exists.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Penetration test**: an authorised simulated attack. **CVE**: an identifier for a publicly known vulnerability. **CVSS**: a 0–10 severity score. **Attack surface**: everything an attacker could reach. **Bug bounty**: a reward programme for reported flaws.
